title: Who Does More of the Housework?
text:
In 1979 Michael Ross and Fiore Sicoly of the University of Waterloo in Canada asked married couples a simple set of questions, with each spouse answering separately. For a list of everyday activities, such as making breakfast, cleaning the house, shopping for groceries and caring for the children, each person estimated what share of the responsibility was theirs.

When the researchers added up the two spouses' estimates, the totals usually came to more than 100 percent. Each partner tended to believe they did more than their partner thought they did. This was true not only for pleasant or admirable contributions but also for negative ones, such as causing arguments. That suggested the bias was not just self-flattery.

Ross and Sicoly also asked people to recall specific examples of their own and their partner's contributions. Those who could remember more of their own contributions claimed a larger share. They argued that the root of the problem is memory. We witness every one of our own efforts, while we see only some of our partner's, and our own are easier to recall. Similar patterns appeared in other groups, including basketball players, whose memories of a game favored their own team's actions.
lesson: You probably notice your own contributions far more than other people's. Before arguing about who does more, assume you are missing some of what the other person does.
source: Ross, M., and Sicoly, F. (1979). Egocentric biases in availability and attribution. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 37(3), 322-336.
